design-code.name: East Riding Design Code
design-code.description: The East Riding Design Code has been prepared to clarify design expectations and improve the quality of new development across the whole of the East Riding of Yorkshire.
design-code.vision: Green, inclusive and distinctive places, which connect landscape, people, place and nature. New development in the East Riding will celebrate the diversity of the built and natural environment and its heritage to create healthy and sustainable places for the communities of today and tomorrow.
design-code.coverage: The whole of the East Riding of Yorkshire
design-code.credits: Illustrations by Harper Perry Ltd; Illustrations by Joseph Cox, FORM Studio

design-code-chapters.name: Codes and Guidance: Environment
design-code-chapters.intro-text: Land within a site must meet multiple requirements. Consideration should be given early in the design process as to how biodiversity net gain, green infrastructure, drainage, public open space, and movement corridors can work together to make the best use of land within the site. Environmental concerns are as important for large strategic sites as they are for extensions to existing developments.

design-code-sections.name: Green Infrastructure
design-code-sections.intro-text: Green infrastructure provides multiple benefits using nature-based solutions. It helps nature to thrive creating prosperous communities and beautiful places that improve our connection with nature and contribute to well-being and healthier lifestyles. It supports natural habitats and biodiversity, improves water quality and creates resilience to climate change. It is important that green infrastructure is designed to maximise these benefits throughout the site.

design-code-sections.name: Biodiversity
design-code-sections.intro-text:
Biodiversity is essential for a healthy environment that is resilient to climate change and supports healthier environments for people.

Policy requires that biodiversity net gain (BNG) be achieved with new development. It is important that this is done in a way that integrates with blue and green infrastructure, public open space and movement networks.

design-code-sections.name: Trees and Hedgerows
design-code-sections.intro-text: Trees and Hedgerows are a significant part of the natural environment. They contribute greatly to a high-quality built environment, providing multiple benefits. Planting trees along streets helps slow down cars protecting more vulnerable users, helps improve air quality, and reduce noise levels. Trees also help mitigate climate change effects by capturing and storing atmospheric carbon, managing rainwater, reducing flood risk and minimising urban heat effects. Trees create beautiful landscapes that provide a place for recreation and relaxation.

design-code-sections.name: Sustainable Drainage
design-code-sections.intro-text: Sustainable Drainage Systems (SuDS) help mitigate flood risk, moderate microclimate, benefit ecology and biodiversity, and provide water quality benefits alongside conserving water. Whilst providing these functions, SuDS which are integrated into the site can also contribute to creating great places and enhance and influence the character of a development and area.

design-code-sections.name: Renewable Energy
design-code-sections.intro-text:
The impacts of climate change are being felt globally. Integrating renewable and efficient energy supplies are one-way new development can seek to mitigate some of the environmental impact it has.

Renewable energy can be delivered in many ways and at different scales. The heating and energy sources needed for a site must be considered in the early stages of development and integrated into proposals in a way which respects the context and character of the surrounding area.

design-code-rules.title: Retaining and Increasing Trees and Hedgerows
design-code-rules.requirement-text:
Trees and hedgerows should be retained and their provision should be increased wherever possible, for their holistic benefits to the function and performance of both the built and natural environment, as well as physical and mental wellbeing.

Tree planting should reflect native and climate resistant species (see The Trees and Design Action Group, TDAG, for further information).

design-code-rules.title: Tree Retention Requirements
design-code-rules.requirement-text: Existing category A and B trees within the development site must be retained.
design-code-rules.guidance-text: In addition to Category A and B trees, Category C trees should be retained where possible to support biodiversity (see section 3.2 Biodiversity). The removal of any trees must be justified within the supporting documents.

design-code-rules.title: Replacing Removed Trees
design-code-rules.requirement-text: When there is the need to remove existing trees (of any category) they must be replaced on-site on a 1:2 ratio.
design-code-rules.guidance-text:
Replacement trees should be planted no later than the next available planting season upon completion of the relevant phase of development.

The size of tree planted will depend on species selection and location. On streets, extra heavy or heavy standard trees will be the most suitable size for replacement trees. Please contact the local planning authority for pre-application advice if further information is required.

design-code-rules.title: On-Site Renewable Energy Requirement
design-code-rules.requirement-text: At least one form of on-site renewable energy must be delivered where development includes new buildings.
design-code-rules.guidance-text:
The inclusion of on-site renewable energy is part of the councils Climate Change Strategy 2022-2030 to reduce carbon emissions in the authority. This can be done on an individual plot basis or using larger scale solutions to provide heating and energy across a site. When installing renewable technology, it is important that they fit in with the surrounding context and do not look overbearing, are screened from view. and do not cause noise pollution. It is also important to ensure individual buildings are designed to be as energy efficient as possible to make the best use of the energy needed to run them.

Photovoltaic Panels (PV) should be designed holistically with the building form. On roofs that front a street, or are considered visually prominent one or more of the following methods should be used:

- photovoltaic tiles, bonded with the surrounding roof tiling;
- PV’s set into the roof structure where this does not dominate the roof plane.

Where not on visually prominent roofs, methods of fixing other than those listed above can be considered.

Solar Water Heating should be considered in addition to Photovoltaic Panels.

Air Source Heat Pumps should be located where they are not visually prominent from outside of the plot of the building they are connected with. As the screening of heat pumps can impact their use it is recommended they are placed to the side or rear of a building where possible.

The location of pumps in relation to the windows of neighbouring properties, due to noise pollution, should also be considered.

Ground Source Heat Pumps should be considered as an alternative to air source heat pumps to minimise visual impact.

Community heat networks redistribute heat from one place to others and are an efficient way of heating many places from waste heat or a centralised low carbon source.

Small wind energy systems should only be considered where they can be screened from view and do not cause noise pollution.

rows.description: Below ground structures that store water temporarily before infiltration, slow release or connect with rainwater harvesting systems.
benefits: Can store a high volume of water
Installed underground for efficient use of space

rows.description: Shallow planters that pond temporarily and filter the water through vegetation and soil before infiltration or storage. Can be constructed in private gardens, along streets or other public spaces. Rain Gardens are smaller, simple bioretention systems, normally associated with individual properties.
benefits: A range of scales possible
Visual amenity and biodiversity benefits
Slow flow and clean water

rows.description: A roof covered in local soil which is allowed to self seed with local vegetation.
benefits: Ecological benefits
Reduce pollution, noise and energy usage

rows.description: Roofs or walls covered by vegetation that help retain, attenuate and treat runoff.
benefits: Do not need additional land
Visual and ecological benefits
Reduce pollution, noise and energy usage
Can provide some the same health benefits as gardens

rows.description: Dry and shallow basins that can store large amounts of water during events allowing for sediments to settle before infiltration.
benefits: Can be part of multifunctional spaces for recreation
Can include shrubs and trees to improve biodiversity and visual amenity. Planting also helps clean water
Keeps rainfall on-site helping to reduce runoff and prevent flooding

rows.description: Gaps between surface materials allow for the infiltration of water to an underlying layer before infiltration to ground. There are different types of permeable surfaces including paving, gravel and woodchip. Pervious pavements are suitable for pedestrians and vehicle use
benefits: Reduce and slow run-off
Low maintenance
Allow for activity on surface
A choice of materials to fit with the visual amenity of the area

rows.description: Permanent pools with vegetation, that store runoff temporarily for attenuation and treatment, allowing sediments to settle.
benefits: Can vary in scale
Can add to visual amenity
Can incorporate planting to boost biodiversity

rows.description: Systems that collect rainwater within the boundaries of a property to use on-site.
benefits: Use for toilet flushing, irrigation and watering reducing demand for potable water
Keeps rainfall on-site helping to reduce runoff and prevent flooding

rows.description: Hollow underground structures filled with draining material, such as gravel, allow for water collection and slow infiltration. Low maintenance and suitable for gardens.
benefits: Slow the flow of water
Do not occupy surface space
Can be integrated into garden design

rows.description: Shallow, vegetated channels which provide temporary storage, infiltration and conveyance of water.
benefits: Ideal for use along streets and in car parks and other permeable and impermeable surfaces as part of landscaping scheme to improve visual amenity.
Clean surface water run off
Biodiversity benefits (when combined with trees and species rich plants

rows.description: Tree pits can be provided along streets and car parking to collect and attenuate runoff.
benefits: Visual amenity and biodiversity benefits
Can be combined well with other SuDS
Collect, clean and infiltrate surface water run off

rows.description: A smaller scale method of rainwater harvesting. Water butts can be attached to down pipes and used for watering gardens.
benefits: Affordable, simple to build, install and maintain
Reduces need for fresh water for gardening

rows.description: Ponds densely covered with vegetation with shallow areas that allow the plants that are rooted in the bottom to grow enhancing water treatment.
benefits: Visual amenity

glossary-terms.definition: The term given to the variety of life on earth, encompassing all life, from the smallest micro-organisms to the largest mammals and plants.
glossary-terms.extraction-notes: The hyphen in "micro-organisms" falls at a line end in the PDF; it is kept because no line-end hyphen in this PDF splits a single word.

glossary-terms.definition: Biodiversity Net Gain (BNG) is a principle that aims to leave biodiversity in a better state than before. This approach ensures that any development activity results in an overall increase in biodiversity, rather than just mitigating the impacts of the development.

A block is a defined area of land within a settlement that is bounded by streets or other physical boundaries. It is the basic unit of urban land use and typically consists of a collection of buildings.

Character refers to the distinctive and unique qualities that define the identity, atmosphere, and overall feel of a specific area or locality. It encompasses a combination of physical, cultural, historical, and social attributes that give a place its sense of personality, charm, and authenticity.

An area of special architectural or historic interest, the character or appearance of which it is desirable to preserve or enhance. There are over 100 conservation areas in the East Riding. These are shown on the Policies Map.
Context refers to the physical, cultural, historical, and social conditions and elements that surround and influence a particular location or environment.

A Design and Access Statement (DAS) is a document that accompanies planning applications for development proposals in the United Kingdom. It provides a comprehensive explanation and justification of the design principles, rationale, and considerations underlying the proposed development, as well as how the design addresses access requirements and enhances inclusivity.

A type of open space that includes linear features of open character including towpaths, riverbanks, cycle ways and disused railway lines. They are strategically planned and managed to facilitate ecological connectivity, biodiversity conservation, and sustainable urban development.

A network of new and existing multi-functional green space, both rural and urban, which is capable of delivering a wide range of environmental and quality of life benefits for local communities. Includes such as parks, forests, wetlands, green spaces, and water bodies, as well as engineered systems such as green roofs, permeable pavements, rain gardens, and bioswales.
Heritage refers to the legacy of physical artifacts and intangible attributes inherited from past generations, maintained in the present, and preserved for the benefit of future generations.

Landscape refers to the visible features of an area of land, including natural elements such as terrain, vegetation, bodies of water, and climate, as well as human-made elements such as buildings, roads, and infrastructure.

Layout refers to the spatial arrangement or organisation of various elements within a settlement or site. This includes the distribution of buildings, land uses, transportation networks, public spaces, infrastructure and amenities.

A listed building is a structure or building that has been officially designated as having special architectural, historical, or cultural significance. There are three categories of listing in the UK: Grade I (buildings of exceptional interest), Grade II* (particularly important buildings of more than special interest), and Grade II (buildings of special interest).
A microclimate refers to the climate conditions that prevail within a relatively small or localised area, such as a garden, park, street, or building courtyard.
A movement network refers to a structured system or arrangement through which people move from one place to another.

All open space of public value, including land and areas of water (such as rivers, canals, lakes and reservoirs) which offer important opportunities for sport and recreation and can act as a visual amenity.
This is the space that is visible and accessible to members of the public. It includes; streets, pedestrianised areas, promenades, squares, river and sea frontages, parks and areas of open space.
Energy derived from a natural source which can be continually replenished, for example wind or solar power.
Scale refers to the relative size, proportion, and spatial dimensions of elements within the built environment, including buildings, streets, blocks, and entire neighbourhoods.

Surface water runoff refers to the movement of rainwater, snowmelt, or other precipitation over the land surface, eventually flowing into streams, rivers, lakes, or oceans. It occurs when precipitation exceeds the infiltration capacity of the soil or when the ground is saturated.
A wide range of sustainable approaches to surface-water drainage management which aim to mimic natural drainage processes and remove pollutants from urban run-off at source.
glossary-terms.extraction-notes: The hyphen in "surface-water" falls at a line end in the PDF; it is kept because no line-end hyphen in this PDF splits a single word.

glossary-terms.definition: A tree pit is an excavated area in the ground specifically designed to accommodate the planting and growth of trees in built environments.

A view refers to a visual perspective or sightline from a specific vantage point typically encompassing views of natural or built features such as landscapes, landmarks, buildings, public spaces, and streetscapes.
A wildlife network refers to a connected system of natural habitats that facilitates the movement, dispersal, and genetic exchange of wildlife populations within a landscape.
